title.narrative: The Young Women for Awareness, Agency, Advocacy, and Accountability (YW4A) Programme

description.narrative: Influence the adoption, amendment, withdrawal or effective utilisation and implementation of laws and policies towards promoting young women’s rights to leadership, participation and ending SGBV in South Sudan by 2025.

The programme aims to strengthen and diversify young women’s participation and amplify their voices to effectively influence decision-making towards gender-just laws, policies, norms, and practices related to their bodily integrity and equal participation.

title.narrative: WRGE 1.1 (WRG001) # of laws blocked, adopted or improved to eradicate all forms of violence against women and girls in public and private life;

description.narrative: Advocacy towards the enactment of the draft Anti-GBV Bill and Family Law Bill.Involvement in the Permanent Constitution-making process to define marriageable age as over the age of 18 in line with the Child Act and Penal Code Act, improve the provision on customary law and criminalize marital rape by repealing Section 247(3) of the Penal Code Act.

comment.narrative: 1.The Anti-GBV Bill, tabled in Parliament in 2019, aimed at reforming and consolidating the law relating to gender based violence including domestic violence, intimate partner violence, sexual violence and offences, assault, harassment, harmful customary practices, and child protection; to provide for the protection of victims of gender-based violence; constitute the Anti-Gender-Based Violence Committee; establish the Anti-Gender-Based Violence Fund; to establish the Anti-Gender-Based Violence Court; establish the One Stop Centre also known as Family Protection Centre. Under YW4A, we will advocate for the adoption of this Bill and its enactment.2. The Family Law Bill provides for marriage, including setting age of marriage at 18 and above, divorce and succession to property including distribution of property in testate and intestate succession. It is in line with regional and international human rights norms and would solve the challenge brought on by the application of customary law. 3. The Transitional Constitution of South Sudan as amended by the Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of Conflict in South Sudan champions gender equality but allows unwritten customary law and practices and customary courts for each of the 64 tribes significant influence of women, supporting their subordination and discrimination. As the country embarks on the development of a Permanent Constitution, the YW4A programme will engage in the process to (1) advocate for the setting of the minimum age of marriage at 18 in line with the Child Act and other instruments ratified by South Sudan and (2) to define that the applicable customary law is secondary and that which is based on positive customary practices and does not infringe human rights and consequently that customary courts should not adjudicate over cases of SGBV.4. Section 247(3) of the Penal Code Act does not acknowledge marital rape closely tied to customary norms where marriage and dowry payment make a woman the property of the husband.
Enactment of the draft Anti-GBV Billand the Family Law Bill plus Repeal of Section 247(3) of the Penal Code Act on marital rape

Advocacy by the YW4A implementing partners on these three pieces of legislation has largely been conducted together. Various actions since the beginning of the programme, including a series of consultative meetings on the status of the bills in 2024 and 2025, have facilitated constructive engagement with the Ministry of Gender and the Technical Committee of the Ministry of Justice. Drafting of the anti-GBV bill was conducted in 2023 and some revisions in 2024 were made following meetings convened under YW4A. It now seems likely that it may pass in 2025 as it has buy-in and active support from the Ministry of Gender (MoG) and was reviewed and submitted to the Ministry of Justice in early 2025. Subsequently, in June 2025, the Under-Secretary of the MoG confirmed that the bill had been finalised and committed to having it tabled at the Council of Ministers and then Parliament this year.The Family Law bill is less likely to be enacted in the near future as there was still only a zero draft in November 2024 and many more inputs are needed. In early 2025, the minister indicated that the ministry is planning to involve CSOs in the review of the bill. Through SOAWR member SIHA, which is leading national support to the Ministry of Gender in developing the Bill, the WROs and young women have meaningfully participated in review meetings and giving input.The minister also indicated that the article on marital rape in the anti-GBV bill is pending for discussion by the members of legislative assemble once it resumes sitting. Subsequently, the undersecretary of the MoG reported that legal experts from the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs advised against including a section on marital rape in the Anti-GBV bill, stating that marital rape is already addressed under the Penal Code Act, which takes legal precedence over the Anti-GBV Bill. Therefore, they recommended increased advocacy for an amendment of Section 247 of the Penal Code Act to explicitly criminalize marital rape.The likely extension of the transitional period and consequent postponement of elections for another two years will allow work to continue on these bills, which would otherwise be interrupted.Engage in the permanent Constitution-making process to maintain the age of marriage at 18 and improve the provision on the place of customary law and the role of customary courtsA bill on marriage age was reported as being with the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs at the beginning of 2023 but has not progressed subsequently. This bill is effectively supported through other bills, e.g. anti-GBV, that define adults as 18 years of age or older. As with the anti-GBV bill (see above) there are verbal commitments of support from ministerial representatives, in this case the Minister for the Interior and the Undersecretary of the Ministry of Gender, and the likely extension of the transitional period provides opportunities for the inclusion of young women’s voices through the constitutional process, including the youth constitutional forum.

Reforming gender/sex discriminatorylaws is a long and delicate process.WROs and young women are engagingin legal advocacy in contexts thatare often fragile and characterised asnarrow civic space. As a result, WROsrepresentatives and activists experience backlash from authorities foradvocating for what is often describedas ‘western or foreign values’.

Draft Anti-GBV Bill is currently under review with the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional AffairsFamily Law Bill still with the Ministry of GenderMemorandum jointly submitted by YW4A partners and the Rule of Law Technical Working Group on marital rape.Constitution Making Process Act was assented to by the President, paving the way for the establishment of a team of drafters who are to develop the Permanent Constitution.

Enactment of the draft Anti-GBV BillEnactment of the Family Law BillDefine marriageable age in the draft Permanent Constitution as over the age of 18 in line with the Child Act and Penal Code ActImprove the provisions on the place of customary law to be positive norms that do not contradict human rights and the role of customary courts in the draft Permanent Constitution.Repeal of Section 247(3) of the Penal Code Act on marital rape

WROs and young women have engaged key officials including Ministers and Members of Parliament, in collaboration with coalitions of like-minded organizations and multi-sectoral platforms on gender equality. This has reinvigorated discussions on the enactment of critical laws that have been pending before Parliament. A young women under the programme is also involved in the Permanent Constitution-making process and was part of the team that validated the Bill. Partners additionally with the Rule of Law Technical Reference Group of the GBV Sub-Cluster, developed and submitted a position paper on marital rape.

description.narrative: Advocacy towards the adoption of the Girl Child Education Bill in Western Equatorial State

comment.narrative: The Girl Child Education Bill has been drafted and tabled many times before the Central Equatorial State Legislative Assembly since 2014. The Bill promotes education of the girl child as an affirmative action of the State and provides a legal framework to protect young schoolgirls from sexual abuse, early marriages and early pregnancies. The YW4A programme will advocate for the adoption of the Bill to support the existing legal framework and ensure that the right to education for girls is fulfilled and protected.
Adoption of Girl Child Education Bill in Western Equatorial State

As of late 2024, this bill appeared to be close to approval as it had received widespread support, including from the Minister of General Education and Instruction and the Speaker of the legislative assembly. Unfortunately, the bill was not debated by the State Legislative Assembly because the Governor was removed from office before the Assembly could convene for the debate. As of early 2025, an Acting Governor was in place and granted authorization for the Legislative Assembly to be mobilized and resume its sessions. The Assembly began sitting during Q2 and the Deputy Speaker confirmed that this bill is among the pending bills expected to be tabled for discussion.
no changes on target value
The Girl Child Education Bill was passed by the State Executive and is in the State Legislative Assembly

WROs and young women in the Central Equatorial State have advocated with the executive and Legislative Assembly on the engactment of the Bill. A revised draft was tabled before the Legislative Assembly for consideration.

description.narrative: WRGE 2.1 (WRG016) Advocacy towards better implementation of the 35% gender representation under the Transitional Constitution

comment.narrative: Article 16 (4)(a) of the Transitional Constitution read together with Section 110 (3) & (4)(a) of the Local Government Act, 2009 (LGA) mandates all levels of government to promote women participation in public life and their representation in the legislative and executive organs by at least twenty-five per cent as an affirmative action to redress imbalances created by history, customs, and traditions. This position of the constitutional mandate on affirmative action has further been strengthened by Chapter I of Revitalized Agreement Paragraph 1.4.4 which states that “provisions of the Transitional Constitution of the Republic of South Sudan and R-ARCSS on participation of women (35%) in the Executive shall be observed. Under Chapter V of the Agreement and specifically paragraph 5.1.1, upon establishment, the government shall initiate legislation for the establishment of the following transitional justice institutions and observe the 35% women representations in these institutions. Under YW4A, we will call for the implementation of this quota, which has not been met, and encourage young women to take up leadership positions and run for elective office.
Better implementation of the 35% gender equality representation under the Transitional Constitution
35% representation Gender Equality provision under the Transitional Constitution
Advocacy towards better implementation of the 35% gender representation under the Transitional Constitution
Better implementation of 35% representation / Gender Equality provision under the Transitional Constitution

Evidence of progress is very limited and the lack of elections reduces opportunities for these provisions to be tested. A survey of young women involved with YW4A provided some encouraging signs of political participation and their interest in future participation. Unfortunately, the number of responses was very low and they appear to have come from some of the most active young women working with the programme.Positively, a Women’s Leadership and Empowerment Bill has been developed and YW4A participants were involved in its review, including in settings with SOAWR member SIHA. The Bill provides a framework for the implementation of the 35% affirmative action representation and provides for women’s participation in decision-making and leadership. The Minister for Gender indicated, in early 2025, that it is pending for discussion by the members of Legislative Assembly; as of July 2025, Parliament had begun sitting again but the legislative agenda was still pending.

description.narrative: Advocacy towards the ratification of the Maputo Protocol and the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child.

comment.narrative: South Sudan signed the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child and parliament approved the ratification of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (Maputo Protocol) but is yet to deposit its instruments of ratification. We will join the advocacy efforts in calling for the ratification of these critical treaties that have immense potential in protecting the rights of women and girls in South Sudan.
4b) Official ratification of Maputo Protocol; the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child; 35% representation Gender Equality provision under the Transitional Constitution
Maputo Protocol ratified and instruments of ratification officially deposited with the African Union Commission
Official ratification of the Maputo Protocol

The Maputo Protocol was signed by the president during Q1 of 2023 and the ratification process formally concluded during Q2 of that year. This stood out among achievements where YW4A advocacy efforts, together with other actors’ voices, were heard. During 2022, the YW4A partners in South Sudan participated in build-up to the planned ratification mission by the SOAWR Coalition supported by the Equality Now and STEWARDWOMEN. This involved a series of constructive dialogues with government actors and CSOs under the auspices of the Coalition of Civil Society Organisations on the Ratification of Maputo Protocol in South Sudan (CCORPS), which had been advocating for ratification since 2013. YW4A partners were involved in deliberations and YWCA South Sudan, Centre for Inclusive Governance Peace and Justice (CIGPJ) and one young woman were appointed to a committee tasked with following up on the status of the Protocol with the National Legislative Assembly and the Ministries for Gender and Justice.Work has not stopped on this following ratification. Participants in the young women’s workshop indicated that one of the things they are more likely to carry on doing after the end of YW4A will be advocacy for domestication of the Protocol. In the Q2 2025 Equality Now report, it was indicated that, as a result of advocacy by YW4A and other SOAWR partners and WROs, the MoG Gender is planning to develop a National Action Plan for the implementation of the Protocol, which will include the legal advocacy priorities under YW4A and legislation to advance women rights.Official ratification of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the ChildThe Ministry of Gender restarted the process in 2024 but late that year it appeared unlikely to be achieved in the near future, not only because the process has gone back to the beginning but because of other government priorities.
Ratification of the Maputo ProtocolRatification of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child
The President of the Republic of South Sudan signed the Maputo Protocol and the instrument of ratification was deposited at the African Union in June 2023.
